entry:
European intellectual and cultural movement of the late 17th and 18th centuries, marked by an emphasis on reason, empirical evidence, and the scientific method. Also called the Age of Reason, it emerged in western and central Europe, reached its peak in the 18th century, and spread to the European colonies in the Americas and Oceania.

The movement grew out of the [[Scientific Revolution]], whose figures included Galileo, Francis Bacon, and [[Isaac Newton|Newton]]. Philosophical foundations were laid by Descartes, Hobbes, Spinoza, and [[John Locke|Locke]]. Dating varies: some historians begin the period with Descartes' *Discourse on the Method* (1637), others with Newton's *Principia Mathematica* (1687). Traditional European chronology runs from the death of Louis XIV in 1715 to the [[French Revolution]] in 1789, though many historians now extend it into the early 19th century.

Ideas circulated through scientific academies, literary salons, coffeehouses, Masonic lodges, and an expanding print culture. Among the best known publications was the [[Encyclopédie]] (1751–72, 35 volumes), compiled by Diderot, d'Alembert, and about 150 others. Other landmark works include Montesquieu's *The Spirit of the Laws* (1748), Rousseau's *The Social Contract* (1762), and Adam Smith's *The Wealth of Nations* (1776). [[Immanuel Kant|Kant]]'s essay *Answering the Question: What Is Enlightenment?* gave the movement its motto, *sapere aude* ("dare to know").

Central doctrines were individual liberty, representative government, the rule of law, and religious tolerance, in contrast to absolute monarchy and religious persecution. Some currents went further, arguing for [[Deism]] or atheism, secular states, and the suppression of religious orders, including the Jesuits. Critics, whom Isaiah Berlin later termed the "Counter-Enlightenment," defended traditional religious and political authority against rationalist critique,.

Its ideas weakened the authority of monarchies and established churches and helped prepare the political revolutions of the 18th and 19th centuries. Liberalism, socialism, and neoclassicism all trace their intellectual heritage to it.

Process of becoming older, in which an organism accumulates changes over time and its functions decline. The term refers mainly to humans, many other animals, and fungi; bacteria, perennial plants, and some simple animals are potentially biologically immortal, though evidence of ageing has been reported in the bacterium *Escherichia coli* and in yeast.

In humans, aging comprises physical, psychological, and social change. Reaction time may slow while knowledge accumulates. Of roughly 150,000 people who die each day worldwide, about two-thirds die of age-related causes. Typical changes include falling female fertility after age 35, presbyopia by age 45–50, and [[Menopause|menopause]] between ages 44 and 58. Osteoarthritis incidence reaches 53% at ages 60–64 and [[Dementia|dementia]] affects about 3% of people aged 65–74, 19% of those aged 75–84, and nearly half of those over 85. [[Atherosclerosis]] is classed as an ageing disease and leads to cardiovascular disease, the most common cause of death worldwide. Maximum human lifespan is suggested to be about 115 years; the oldest person recognized by the *Guinness Book of Records* was [[Jeanne Calment]], who reached 122.

Theories fall into two groups. Damage theories hold that accumulating harm, such as DNA oxidation, causes biological systems to fail; programmed theories hold that internal processes, such as epigenetic maintenance, inherently cause ageing. Programmed ageing is distinct from programmed cell death (apoptosis). Evolutionary accounts treat ageing as a by-product of [[Natural selection|natural selection]] favoring early-life fitness. Researchers have catalogued twelve proposed hallmarks of ageing, including [[Stem cell|stem cell]] exhaustion, and debate which are causes and which are correlates.

Normal human cells in culture die after about 50 divisions (the Hayflick limit, discovered 1961), whereas cancer cells and germ cells can be effectively immortal. In nematodes, flies, and mice, caloric restriction and genetic changes extend healthy lifespan; interventions in humans remain largely preclinical.

Cultivation of plants and raising of animals to produce food, fibers, fuels, and raw materials. Broader definitions include forestry and aquaculture.

Agriculture was a key factor in the rise of sedentary human [[Civilization|civilization]], since farming of domesticated plants and animals created food surpluses that allowed people to live in cities. Humans gathered wild grains from at least 105,000 years ago, but deliberate planting began only about 11,500 years ago. Sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle were domesticated about 10,000 years ago. Crops were independently developed in at least 11 regions of the world. The word derives from Latin *agricultura*, from *ager* ("field") and *cultura* ("cultivation").

Regional beginnings differ. Rice was domesticated in southern China, cattle from the wild [[Aurochs|aurochs]] in what is now Turkey and Pakistan, and pigs from wild boar in Eurasia. In the Andes, the potato, beans, coca, llamas, alpacas, and guinea pigs were domesticated; in [[Mesoamerica]], the wild grass teosinte was bred into [[Maize|maize]] between 10,000 and 6,000 years ago; sugarcane was domesticated in New Guinea and sorghum in the Sahel. The horse was domesticated on the Eurasian Steppe around 3500 BC. The Sumerians, relying on the Tigris and Euphrates and a canal system for [[Irrigation|irrigation]], had ploughs by about 3000 BC, and Egyptian farming depended on the Nile's seasonal flooding. China had a nationwide granary system from the 5th century BC and iron-share heavy ploughs by the late 2nd century. The Aztecs built terraces and artificial islands called chinampas.

Major products are foods (cereals, vegetables, fruits, cooking oils, meat, milk, eggs), fibers, fuels, and raw materials such as rubber and timber. Annual output is about 11 billion tonnes of food, 32 million tonnes of natural fiber, and 4 billion m³ of wood; roughly 14% of food is lost before reaching retail. As of 2021, small farms of one hectare or less produced about a third of the world's food, while the 1% of farms larger than 50 hectares held more than 70% of farmland.

In the 20th century, industrial agriculture based on large monocultures came to dominate output. Plant breeding, fertilizers, pesticides, and mechanization sharply raised yields, and advocates credit these advances, often grouped as the [[Green Revolution]], with averting famine and supporting population growth. Critics and researchers also link intensive agriculture to [[Deforestation|deforestation]], depletion of aquifers, antibiotic resistance, pollution, biodiversity loss, and contributions to climate change, while agriculture is itself sensitive to soil degradation, desertification, and a changing climate. Genetically modified organisms are widely used, although some countries ban them, and the use of pesticides and animal-husbandry methods remains debated on environmental and animal-welfare grounds.

Vehicle or machine that flies by gaining support from the air. An aircraft counters gravity with static lift or the dynamic lift of an airfoil, or, in a few cases, with direct downward thrust from its engines. Examples include airplanes, drones, rotorcraft such as [[Helicopter|helicopters]], airships, gliders, and hot-air balloons. Aircraft are classified by lift type, propulsion, and use; a crewed craft has an onboard pilot, while an [[Unmanned aerial vehicle|unmanned aerial vehicle]] is remotely controlled or autonomous.

Lighter-than-air craft, or aerostats, float by buoyancy in cells filled with helium, hydrogen, or hot air. Heavier-than-air craft, or aerodynes, are denser than air and must generate lift, either aerodynamically, with air flowing past a wing, or by powered lift from downward engine thrust.

Kites flown in China several hundred years BC are considered the earliest man-made flight. In the 15th century [[Leonardo da Vinci]] designed flying machines that proved unworkable. The [[Montgolfier brothers]] invented the hot-air balloon in the late 18th century, and the discovery of hydrogen led to the hydrogen balloon; France established military balloon companies during the [[French Revolution]]. Advances in fluid dynamics and Newton's laws of motion produced modern aerodynamics, notably through George Cayley.

The [[Wright brothers]] built and flew the first airplane in 1903, after research on wing design and aircraft control. Their flight of December 17 at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, covered 120 feet in 12 seconds. Rigid airships pioneered by Ferdinand von Zeppelin dominated long-distance flight until the 1930s, when large flying boats took over trans-oceanic routes. After [[World War II]], land-based airplanes replaced flying boats, made more capable first by improved propeller engines and then by jet engines, which transformed civilian air travel and military aviation. Digital electronics later brought fly-by-wire systems, and pilotless drones now serve military, commercial, and recreational purposes.

Third Mughal emperor of India (r. 1556–1605), known as Akbar the Great. He succeeded his father, [[Humayun]], at age 13 under the regency of Bairam Khan.

Born in exile at Amarkot in Sindh, Akbar was raised in Kabul and never learned to read or write. He took the throne in 1556 while the Mughals were fighting the Sur dynasty for Delhi and Agra. Over his reign he enlarged the [[Mughal Empire]] to cover much of the [[Indian subcontinent]] by military campaigns, including conquests of [[Gujarat]] in 1572 and [[Bengal]] in 1576, supported by artillery, matchlocks, and war elephants. Some conquests brought harsh reprisals; after the 1568 siege of Chittor he reportedly ordered the killing of about 30,000 mostly noncombatant Rajputs.

To unify the state, Akbar built a centralized administration and conciliated defeated rulers through marriage and diplomacy. He introduced the mansabdari system, a hierarchy of military and civil ranks, and in 1579–80 standardized land revenue through detailed surveys, building on the precedents of Sher Shah Suri. To maintain peace in a religiously diverse empire he abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1564 and appointed non-Muslims to high civil and military posts. From 1575 he convened debates among scholars of many faiths at the Ibadatkhana, and he promoted a policy of universal peace (*sulh-i kul*).

Disillusioned with orthodox [[Islam]], he promulgated *Din-i Ilahi* (c. 1582), a syncretic creed drawing mainly on Islam and Hinduism, with elements of Zoroastrianism and Christianity. It attracted few followers beyond the court, and orthodox critics viewed his religious policies as heretical.

His courts at Delhi, Agra, and Fatehpur Sikri drew poets, architects, artisans, and holy men, and a distinctive Mughal style of painting and architecture blended Timurid and Perso-Islamic traditions with Indian elements. His vizier Abul Fazl chronicled the reign in the *Akbarnama*. His son Salim, later Jahangir, succeeded him.

Persian-descended mathematician, astronomer, and geographer of the [[Islamic Golden Age]]. Full name Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi. He wrote in Arabic and worked from about 820 at the [[House of Wisdom]] in [[Baghdad]], capital of the [[Abbasid Caliphate]], as astronomer and head of its library.

Little is known with certainty of his life. His name means "from Khwarazm," a region now in Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, though some accounts place his birth near Baghdad. The sources differ on whether he was a Zoroastrian by background; a pious preface to his algebra indicates he was a Muslim. Most of his work dates from 813 to 833.

His treatise *Al-Jabr* (*The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing*) gave the first systematic solution of linear and quadratic equations, solving quadratics by completing the square and supplying geometric justifications. Because he treated [[Algebra|algebra]] as an independent discipline and introduced the methods of "reduction" and "balancing," he has been called the father or founder of algebra; the word derives from *al-jabr* in the title. Translated into Latin by Robert of Chester in 1145, the book served as the principal mathematics textbook of European universities until the 16th century.

His book on Indian arithmetic, written about 825, spread the Hindu–Arabic numeral system through the Middle East and Europe. Its 12th-century Latin translation, *Algoritmi de numero Indorum*, introduced the decimal positional system to the West, and his Latinized name, Algoritmi, is the origin of the word [[Algorithm|algorithm]].

He also revised Ptolemy's *Geography*, listing the longitudes and latitudes of cities and localities, and produced astronomical tables based on Indian and Greek sources, as well as works on the calendar, the astrolabe, and the sundial. His sine and cosine tables made important contributions to trigonometry.

English mathematician, logician, and cryptanalyst, widely regarded as the father of theoretical computer science. In his 1936 paper "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem," he formalized algorithm and computation through the [[Turing machine]], a model of a general-purpose computer,.

Born in London, Turing graduated from King's College, Cambridge, and earned a doctorate from [[Princeton University]] in 1938. During [[World War II]] he worked at Bletchley Park, Britain's codebreaking center, where he headed Hut 8 and focused on German naval messages. His techniques improved on the prewar Polish *bomba* method and hastened the breaking of the [[Enigma machine|Enigma]] cipher. The resulting intelligence, known as Ultra, aided the Allies in the [[Battle of the Atlantic]]. His wartime work, covered by the Official Secrets Act, went unrecognized in his lifetime.

After the war he joined the National Physical Laboratory, where he designed the Automatic Computing Engine, an early stored-program computer. From 1948 he worked at the University of Manchester, contributing to early Manchester computers. His 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" proposed an imitation game, later called the [[Turing test]], as a criterion for machine intelligence and helped found the philosophy of [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]]. He also turned to mathematical biology, studying the chemical basis of morphogenesis through reaction–diffusion models, a field that gave rise to the Turing pattern concept.

In 1952, after acknowledging a sexual relationship with another man, Turing was prosecuted for gross indecency. He received probation conditional on chemical castration and lost his security clearance. He died of cyanide poisoning in 1954, and an inquest ruled the death a suicide; some biographers have questioned that verdict. Following a 2009 campaign, Prime Minister Gordon Brown apologized for "the appalling way [Turing] was treated," and in 2013 Queen Elizabeth II granted him a pardon.

German-born theoretical physicist, best known for developing the theory of relativity. He also made major contributions to [[Quantum mechanics|quantum theory]], and his mass–energy equivalence formula, E = mc², arising from special relativity, has been called the world's most famous equation. He received the 1921 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics for his discovery of the law of the [[Photoelectric effect|photoelectric effect]].

Einstein was born in Ulm in the Kingdom of Württemberg and grew up in Munich. He studied at the Swiss federal polytechnic school in Zurich, became a Swiss citizen in 1901, worked at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern, and received a doctorate in 1905. In 1914 he moved to Berlin to join the Prussian Academy of Sciences. When [[Adolf Hitler]] came to power in 1933, Einstein remained in the U.S., and he became a citizen in 1940. Shortly before [[World War II]] he endorsed a letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt urging American nuclear research, later carried out as the [[Manhattan Project]]. He advocated pacifism and civil rights and supported Zionism.

In 1905, his *annus mirabilis*, he published four papers that outlined a theory of the photoelectric effect, explained Brownian motion, introduced special relativity, and demonstrated the equivalence of mass and energy. In 1915 he proposed general relativity, extending mechanics to include gravitation. A 1917 paper applying it to the universe as a whole introduced the [[Cosmological constant|cosmological constant]] and is regarded as the first step in modern theoretical cosmology. A 1917 paper introduced stimulated emission, the basis of the laser. His work on radiation, in which light consists of particles later called photons, and his collaboration with Satyendra Nath Bose laid the groundwork for Bose–Einstein statistics.

In later decades he objected to the fundamental randomness of quantum theory ("God does not play dice") and sought a unified field theory joining gravitation and electromagnetism. Neither effort succeeded, and he became increasingly isolated from mainstream physics. The element einsteinium is named for him.

Drink containing ethanol, produced by yeast fermentation of sugars from grains, fruits, or other plant materials. Alcoholic beverages are typically divided into beers, wines, and spirits, with alcohol content usually between 3% and 50% by volume; fermented drinks such as beer and wine generally run from 4% to 15%, while distilled spirits such as [[Rum|rum]] and [[Vodka|vodka]] often exceed 40%. Production begins with making sugars available, then fermentation, and for spirits, [[Distillation|distillation]].

The oldest verifiable brewery, in a burial cave near Haifa, Israel, contained residue of 13,000-year-old beer, probably used in ritual feasts. Residues in pottery jars from Jiahu, in China's Henan province, show that a fermented drink of grape, hawthorn fruit, honey, and rice was made about 7000–5600 BC. The earliest evidence of winemaking, from about 6000 BC, comes from Georgia in the South Caucasus, and the earliest clear chemical evidence of barley beer, about 3500–3100 BC, from Godin Tepe in the Zagros Mountains of Iran. In Egypt wine was reserved for royalty and the elite, while beer was the drink of common people; Sumerian society regulated alcohol and used it in offerings to the gods.

Alcohol is a depressant of the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]]. Low doses cause euphoria, reduced anxiety, and sociability; higher doses cause drunkenness, stupor, unconsciousness, or death. Long-term use can lead to [[Alcoholism|alcoholism]], physical dependence, cardiovascular disease, and several cancers, and alcohol is classified as a group 1 carcinogen. In 2023 the [[World Health Organization]] stated that health risk begins "from the first drop." Alcohol use is linked to about 2.6 million deaths a year.

About a third of humans drink alcohol, averaging about 5.5 liters of pure alcohol a year per adult. The industry exceeded $1.5 trillion in 2017. Most countries regulate production, sale, and consumption, and a few ban it; the temperance movement campaigns against it.

King of Macedon (r. 336–323 BC) who conquered the Achaemenid Persian Empire and created one of the largest empires of antiquity. By the age of 30 his realm stretched from Greece to Egypt and northwestern India. He was undefeated in battle and is widely considered one of history's most successful military commanders.

Born at Pella, son of Philip II and his fourth wife, Olympias, Alexander was tutored by [[Aristotle]] until age 16. He took the throne at 20 after his father's assassination, campaigned in the Balkans, destroyed Thebes, and assumed leadership of the League of Corinth. In 334 BC he began a pan-Hellenic invasion of the [[Achaemenid Empire]] that lasted ten years. After conquering Asia Minor and winning decisive battles at Issus and Gaugamela, he overthrew Darius III and took the whole empire. He invaded India in 326 BC and defeated the king Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes, but his troops mutinied and he turned back at the Beas River. He died at [[Babylon]] in 323 BC, the city he had planned as his capital, leaving no clear successor.

His policy of bringing Persian nobles into his court and adopting eastern customs caused resentment among Macedonian veterans. After his death civil wars among his generals, the Diadochi, broke up the empire and began the [[Hellenistic period]]. He founded more than 20 cities, the most prominent being [[Alexandria]] in Egypt, and spread Greek colonies and culture, giving rise to syncretic forms such as Greco-Buddhism and Hellenistic Judaism. Greek became the region's [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] and the main language of the Byzantine Empire until 1453. Ancient accounts, preserved mainly in later works by Arrian and Plutarch, mix fact with legend. He became a legendary hero akin to [[Achilles]]; his tactics are still studied in military academies.
